source_evidence.observation: A random variable X satisfying one of properties (i)–(iv) of Proposition 2.5.2 is called sub-gaussian, and its sub-gaussian norm is denoted ‖X‖_{ψ₂}.
The displayed definition is ‖X‖_{ψ₂} = inf {t > 0 : E exp(X²/t²) ≤ 2}.
Property (iv) is the existence of K₄ > 0 such that E exp(X²/K₄²) ≤ 2.

source_evidence.anchor: Proposition 2.5.2, opening sentence and clause preceding property (v)
source_evidence.observation: Properties (i)–(iv) are equivalent for a general random variable X; the additional mean-zero assumption appears only when property (v) is included.

The source remarks that the constant 2 in some properties of Proposition 2.5.2 has no special meaning and can be replaced by another absolute constant larger than 1, although Equation (2.13) itself fixes the threshold at 2.
The following exercise describes ‖·‖_{ψ₂} as a norm on the space of sub-gaussian random variables.

binders: X is a random variable satisfying one, hence any, of the equivalent properties (i)–(iv) of Proposition 2.5.2. [PDF page 16; printed page 27; anchor: Definition 2.5.6]
t is the scale variable bound inside the infimum and is restricted by t > 0. [PDF page 16; printed page 27; anchor: Equation (2.13)]
hypotheses: X is sub-gaussian in the enclosing definition, meaning that X satisfies one of the equivalent properties (i)–(iv) of Proposition 2.5.2. [PDF page 16; printed page 27; anchor: Definition 2.5.6]
Equivalently for the property used by the definition, there exists K₄ > 0 such that E exp(X²/K₄²) ≤ 2. [PDF page 13; printed page 24; anchor: Proposition 2.5.2(iv)]
conclusions: The sub-gaussian norm of X is exactly ‖X‖_{ψ₂} = inf {t > 0 : E exp(X²/t²) ≤ 2}. [PDF page 16; printed page 27; anchor: Equation (2.13)]
The notation ‖X‖_{ψ₂} denotes the sub-gaussian norm introduced in Definition 2.5.6. [PDF page 16; printed page 27; anchor: Definition 2.5.6]
definitions_and_conventions: The right-hand side is an infimum over all positive scales t satisfying the exponential-moment bound, rather than an arbitrary witness of that bound. [PDF page 16; printed page 27; anchor: Equation (2.13)]
The admissibility predicate is E exp(X²/t²) ≤ 2, with X squared before division by t² and application of the exponential. [PDF page 16; printed page 27; anchor: Equation (2.13)]
The threshold in the displayed norm definition is the literal constant 2. [PDF page 16; printed page 27; anchor: Equation (2.13)]

Property (iv)'s parameter K₄ has the same scale role that t has in the infimum formula. [PDF page 13; printed page 24; anchor: Proposition 2.5.2(iv); PDF page 16; printed page 27; anchor: Equation (2.13)]
implicit_context: No assumption E X = 0 is required for properties (i)–(iv) or for Definition 2.5.6; mean zero is introduced only for equivalence with property (v). [PDF page 13; printed page 24; anchor: Proposition 2.5.2, clause preceding property (v)]
The displayed quantity is presented on the space of sub-gaussian random variables. [PDF page 16; printed page 27; anchors: Definition 2.5.6 and Exercise 2.5.7]

Because property (iv) holds for the X under discussion, the set of admissible positive scales in Equation (2.13) is nonempty. [PDF page 13; printed page 24; anchor: Proposition 2.5.2(iv); PDF page 16; printed page 27; anchor: Definition 2.5.6]

details: X is the random variable whose sub-gaussian size is measured, while t is a positive candidate scale over which an infimum is taken. [PDF page 16; printed page 27; anchors: Definition 2.5.6 and Equation (2.13)]
The norm is determined by the lower boundary, expressed as an infimum, of the positive scales satisfying the exponential-moment inequality. [PDF page 16; printed page 27; anchor: Equation (2.13)]
Admissibility depends on the expectation of exp(X²/t²), not on a pointwise bound for X and not on E exp(X/t). [PDF page 16; printed page 27; anchor: Equation (2.13)]
The norm carries the ψ₂ index, the scale is squared in the denominator, X is squared in the exponent, and the comparison threshold is 2. [PDF page 16; printed page 27; anchor: Equation (2.13)]
Centering is not part of this definition; E X = 0 is needed only for the separate MGF property (v). [PDF page 13; printed page 24; anchor: Proposition 2.5.2, clause preceding property (v)]

Although Proposition 2.5.2 compares its parameters only up to absolute constant factors and Remark 2.5.3 says the threshold 2 is not intrinsically special, Equation (2.13) defines this particular norm by an exact equality using threshold 2. [PDF page 13; printed page 24; anchor: Proposition 2.5.2 and footnote 4; PDF page 15; printed page 26; anchor: Remark 2.5.3; PDF page 16; printed page 27; anchor: Equation (2.13)]

undebatable_constraints: The left-hand side must be the sub-gaussian norm ‖X‖_{ψ₂}. [PDF page 16; printed page 27; anchors: Definition 2.5.6 and Equation (2.13)]
The right-hand side must be an infimum over scales satisfying t > 0. [PDF page 16; printed page 27; anchor: Equation (2.13)]
The qualifying condition must be E exp(X²/t²) ≤ 2. [PDF page 16; printed page 27; anchor: Equation (2.13)]
The equality is exact; it is not merely an inequality or an equivalence up to an unspecified constant. [PDF page 16; printed page 27; anchor: Equation (2.13)]
The enclosing scope is a sub-gaussian random variable X, characterized by properties (i)–(iv). [PDF page 16; printed page 27; anchor: Definition 2.5.6]

No mean-zero, independence, or identical-distribution hypothesis belongs to Equation (2.13). [PDF page 13; printed page 24; anchor: Proposition 2.5.2 and its separate mean-zero clause for property (v); PDF page 16; printed page 27; anchor: Definition 2.5.6]

The literal threshold used in Equation (2.13) is 2, even though a neighboring remark discusses alternative absolute thresholds for equivalent sub-gaussian properties. [PDF page 15; printed page 26; anchor: Remark 2.5.3; PDF page 16; printed page 27; anchor: Equation (2.13)]

ambiguities.issue: The prose says that the norm is the “smallest K₄,” whereas the displayed equation defines it as an infimum and does not separately assert that the infimum is attained.
ambiguities.evidence: Definition 2.5.6 uses the phrase “smallest K₄ in property iv” immediately before Equation (2.13), whose structural operator is inf. [PDF page 16; printed page 27; anchors: Definition 2.5.6 and Equation (2.13)]
ambiguities.impact: A faithful statement should encode the displayed infimum and should not add a minimizer-attainment assertion absent from the selected passage. [PDF page 16; printed page 27; anchor: Equation (2.13)]

ambiguities.issue: The source does not specify an extended-real value or an empty-set convention for applying the displayed formula to a non-sub-gaussian random variable.
ambiguities.evidence: Definition 2.5.6 first restricts attention to X satisfying properties (i)–(iv), and Exercise 2.5.7 calls this a norm on the space of sub-gaussian random variables. [PDF page 16; printed page 27; anchors: Definition 2.5.6 and Exercise 2.5.7]
ambiguities.impact: The contract does not infer a source-defined value for arbitrary non-sub-gaussian random variables; any such extension would require an additional convention not stated here. [PDF page 16; printed page 27; anchors: Definition 2.5.6 and Equation (2.13)]

contract_plain_english: For a sub-gaussian random variable X, its ψ₂ norm is the infimum of all positive scales t for which the exponential second-moment expression E exp(X²/t²) is at most 2. No centering assumption is part of this definition. [PDF page 16; printed page 27; anchors: Definition 2.5.6 and Equation (2.13); PDF page 13; printed page 24; anchor: Proposition 2.5.2]
